Information Theory for Engineers

SHANNON, Claude Elwood.

Communication in the Presence of Noise.

New York: The Institute of Radio Engineers, Inc., 1949. $8,500

First edition, the rare author’s offprint, and Claude E. Shannon’s own file copy — the paper that carried information theory out of mathematics and into engineering, and that first set in print three of the results the field still runs on: the geometric proof of the channel-capacity formula C = W log2(1 + S/N), the water-pouring solution for a channel whose noise is uneven across the band, and the first sketch of what became rate-distortion theory. Shannon had founded information theory the year before, but by arguments abstract enough that few practising communication engineers could follow them; here he made the same theory something an engineer could see and use. The copy is unmarked, as he kept it — not a presentation copy sent to a colleague, but the one he retained.

The argument turns on a picture. A signal limited to bandwidth W and duration T is represented as a single point in a space of 2WT dimensions, its coordinates the values of the signal read off at intervals of 1/2W seconds; transmission displaces that point by a noise vector, and reception is the problem of deciding which point was sent. For Gaussian noise the received point falls, with near-certainty, on a thin spherical shell about the transmitted one, so that the number of messages that can be told apart is simply the number of such noise-spheres that pack into the larger sphere of all possible received signals — and counting them gives the capacity. The result ran against the engineering intuition of the day, which held that driving the error rate down must cost transmission rate; Shannon called it ‘a rather surprising result’ and showed instead that any rate below the capacity can be reached with as few errors as one likes, provided the codes are made long enough. It is the channel-coding theorem, stated in prose.

That an engineer could follow the geometry is what made the theory usable. John Pierce, Shannon’s colleague at Bell Labs, called it ‘a clear and appealing geometrical derivation’, and the picture of messages as points and codes as sphere-packings became the working language of the field. The capacity it defined set a target approached only slowly: for four decades real systems ran several decibels short of the Shannon limit, and then, in the space of a few years, all but closed the gap. The turbo codes Claude Berrou and Alain Glavieux announced in 1993 came within half a decibel of it; the low-density parity-check codes that followed were driven to within 0.0045 of a decibel by 2001; and the polar codes Erdal Arıkan introduced in 2009 were the first construction proved to reach the bound outright. Polar codes now carry the control channels of every 5G handset, as the turbo codes before them carried the data channels of 4G. A result that can still be named as the target half a century after it is proved is rare in any science.

The paper’s other results have proved as durable. Stated here as Theorem 1 is what is now taught in every signals course as the sampling theorem: a signal containing no frequency higher than W is fixed completely by its values taken 1/2W seconds apart — the bridge by which the continuous world enters the discrete one without loss, beneath digital audio, digital imaging, and every analog-to-digital converter built since. The water-pouring theorem solves the channel whose noise is uneven across the band by allocating transmitter power the way water finds its level against an uneven floor, filling the quietest sub-bands first; it is the analytical foundation of the multi-carrier systems that run digital broadcasting, Wi-Fi, DSL, and 5G. And the closing sections sketch the rate-distortion problem — how few bits suffice to rebuild a source to a prescribed fidelity — which Shannon would work out in full a decade later and which now governs every lossy codec and every compressed image. Three-quarters of a century on, this is still the working mathematics of communication.

The copy’s distinction is that it is Shannon’s own. After his death in 2001 the family papers stayed with his widow, Mary Elizabeth (‘Betty’) Moore Shannon — herself a Bell Labs computer, who had looked up his references and taken down and edited his work, some of his early papers surviving in her hand rather than his — at the house on Upper Mystic Lake in Winchester, Massachusetts that the family called Entropy House. After her death in 2017 the surviving children placed the holdings, some eighty items Shannon had written or co-authored and kept together as his working library, with a single specialist dealer. The present offprint is one of those file copies, unmarked, as he left it; Shannon’s son Andrew confirmed in writing the family ownership of another item from the same cache, anchoring the provenance of the whole.

Offprints of the paper from Shannon’s files are scarce, and copies of any provenance are seldom recorded. A few survive through other hands — one signed on the wrapper by a contemporary MIT communications engineer, others through the general rare-book trade — but none with the author’s-working-files provenance, and the offprint is not separately recorded in the union library catalogues. The paper falls after the effective cutoff of the older science canons; the standard bibliographical reference for it is Hook & Norman, Origins of Cyberspace, where it is number 882, and the IEEE marked it a Classic Paper, reprinting it in full — with an introduction by Aaron Wyner and Shlomo Shamai — in the Proceedings of the IEEE in 1998.

What the paper did was carry information theory across the line from mathematics into engineering. When Robert Gallager — a younger colleague of Shannon’s at MIT — published Information Theory and Reliable Communication in 1968, the book from which a generation of engineers learned the subject, he was setting in order what Shannon had first drawn here in pictures. The channels built ever since — the telephone modem, the mobile call, the link to a spacecraft beyond the planets — run on the capacity this paper taught engineers how to count.

Physical description

The author’s offprint from the Proceedings of the Institute of Radio Engineers, vol. 37, no. 1 (January 1949), with its own printed title-leaf and preserving the journal pagination. 4to (283 × 217 mm), pp. [1], [10], 11–21, [1, blank]. Buff self-wrappers, stapled at the spine. Near fine. Unmarked, consistent with a copy retained in Shannon’s own working files rather than sent to a named recipient.
